paragraph: Angola's [Presidential Decree 46/18 of 14 February 2018](<https://lex.ao/docs/presidente-da-republica/2018/decreto-presidencial-n-o-46-18-de-14-de-fevereiro/>) approves a national plan for interoperability across central and local administration. It makes adherence to the plan mandatory for public administration services. In the last twelve months, a draft Digital Government Law [went to public consultation on 6 May 2026](<https://ima.gov.ao/web/noticias/ima-promove-sessao-de-consulta-publica-sobre-o-anteprojecto-de-lei-do-governo-digital>). It has 107 articles and would frame interoperability between state institutions. The 2018 decree remains the instrument in force. No source found says it requires bodies to share data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what the state already holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

Benin's [Decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020](<https://api.xroad.bj/media/617ac98a74baa_D%C3%A9cret%20n%C2%B02020-209%20du%2018%20mars%202020%20portant%20mise%20en%20place%20de%20la%20Plateforme%20d%27Interop%C3%A9rabilit%C3%A9%20XRoad%20BJ%20(1).pdf>) was issued by the Presidency. It sets up XRoad BJ, the national interoperability platform through which public bodies exchange data. No later text is recorded as amending or replacing it, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says the decree obliges ministries and agencies to connect to the platform or to exchange data through it. No public body is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share data or to connect to the exchange platform.

Burkina Faso adopted its general interoperability reference, the Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, by [an order of the Prime Minister dated 23 May 2018](<https://burkina24.com/2019/10/15/burkina-un-referentiel-pour-moderniser-ladministration-publique/>). The order fixes rules that make the information systems of public administrations compatible with each other. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing recorded says the order obliges administrations to exchange data or to connect to a common platform. No administration is named as exchanging data because the order requires it. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another body already holds.

Botswana's [Digital Services Act, 2025 (Act No. 22 of 2025)](<http://www.bocra.org.bw/sites/default/files/sites/default/files/documents/digital_services_ACT.pdf>) was passed by the National Assembly on 14 August 2025 and assented to on 17 October 2025. It says [a public or private body shall avoid collecting information that another body already holds](<http://www.bocra.org.bw/sites/default/files/sites/default/files/documents/digital_services_ACT.pdf>). It starts on a date the minister sets by order in the Gazette. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No regulation, decree or order made under the Act has been found, and no public body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to. Mature would need such a rule, or public bodies named as exchanging data under the Act.

Cote d'Ivoire's [Ordinance 2017-500 of 2 August 2017](<https://anssi.gouv.ci/documents/22/Ordonnance_2017-500_02_ao%C3%BBt_2017_sur_les_eservices.pdf>) was made by the President in the Council of Ministers. Its chapter on interoperability says the state sets up a platform [to which every administrative authority is bound to connect](<https://anssi.gouv.ci/documents/22/Ordonnance_2017-500_02_ao%C3%BBt_2017_sur_les_eservices.pdf>). It also bars an authority from asking a user again for information the administration already holds. No repeal is recorded, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or order applying the ordinance since 2023 has been found. No authority is named as connected to the platform because the ordinance requires it. Mature would need such a decree or order, or authorities named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

In November 2025 the government's digital transformation project described [a draft e-government law on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration](<https://patnuc.cm/2025/11/20/services-publics-et-transparence-les-evolutions-cles-de-la-loi-e-gov/>). The draft would require administrations to make their information systems compatible so that they share data securely. It was examined at a workshop in Ebolowa. No promulgation is recorded, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

Cape Verde's [Council of Ministers Resolution 54/2020](<https://nosi.cv/documents/20121/3048284/Medidas%20de%20Acelera%C3%A7%C3%A3o%20Transforma%C3%A7%C3%A3o%20Digital%20na%20AP%20%282020%29.pdf/c556d060-0549-84e6-f11d-9eaee3e3f9d3>) was approved on 19 March 2020 and took effect in March 2020. It orders a legal diploma on interoperability of public administration systems to be drafted. [Measure g](<https://nosi.cv/documents/20121/3048284/Medidas%20de%20Acelera%C3%A7%C3%A3o%20Transforma%C3%A7%C3%A3o%20Digital%20na%20AP%20%282020%29.pdf/c556d060-0549-84e6-f11d-9eaee3e3f9d3>) says state bodies must share the data a process needs, subject to data protection rules. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source says the diploma has been drafted or passed, and no law is reported to have followed the resolution. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

Algeria's [Presidential Decree 25-320 of 30 December 2025](<https://www.joradp.dz/FTP/JO-FRANCAIS/2025/F2025087.pdf>) sets up a national data governance system with a national interoperability system. In the last twelve months it was published and, in September 2026, [a further decree on a secure digital interoperability plan was reported as being drawn up](<https://www.jeune-independant.net/guessoum-sur-lelaboration-dun-decret-sur-linteroperabilite-numerique-permettre-aux-avancees-numeriques-de-produire-pleinement-leurs-effets/>). Before it, [Executive Decree 23-316 of 6 September 2023](<https://www.algerie360.com/les-administrations-nont-plus-le-droit-dexiger-ces-documents-saayoud-promet-des-sanctions-severes/>) was the earlier measure; it remains in force. The 2025 decree makes the system the exclusive channel for exchange between public bodies. No order made under it has been found. Mature would need such an order, or bodies named as exchanging data because the decree requires it.

In December 2025 the chair of Egypt's House ICT committee said the government had [finished a 35-article bill on classifying and circulating information](<https://www.dostor.org/5338473>). The communications minister said that month the draft [would go to Cabinet and then the House](<https://www.fintechgate.net/184454>). In the last twelve months the bill went from a draft, which the deputy communications minister told the committee in February 2024 [had been drafted](<https://www.youm7.com/story/2024/2/12/%D9%88%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%AA%D9%83%D8%B4%D9%81-%D9%84%D9%84%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%A8-%D8%AA%D9%81%D8%A7%D8%B5%D9%8A%D9%84-%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%B9-%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%AC%D8%AF%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%A9-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AF%D9%84/6477784>), to a finished text. The bill has not been passed, and no law is in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

On 28 September 2026 Ethiopia's Council of Ministers [referred a draft National Data Governance Proclamation to the House of Peoples' Representatives](<https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/eng_9629721>). The same meeting is reported as [approving a draft National Data Management Proclamation](<https://www.fanamc.com/english/ethiopias-council-of-ministers-advances-new-legal-frameworks-for-state-institutions-data-sovereignty-defence-and-economy/>), meant to ease data sharing, interoperability and reuse. In the last twelve months these two drafts are the only ones found, and the House had not passed either by the end of September 2026. Neither report states whether it would oblige public bodies to share. No law, decree or regulation on sharing is in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

Gabon's [Ordinance 0006/PR/2025 regulating digitalisation](<https://journal-officiel.ga/21995-0006-pr-2025-/>) was signed by the President on 12 August 2025 and published in the Official Journal on 30 August 2025. It [makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect](<https://www.gabonreview.com/e-gouvernement-le-gabon-se-dote-dun-cadre-juridique-pour-accelerer-la-digitalisation-de-son-administration/>), so that they exchange information, and puts interoperability of information systems at its centre. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or order applying the ordinance has been found, and no administration is named as exchanging data because it requires it. Mature would need such a decree or order, or bodies named as exchanging data because the ordinance requires them to.

Ghana's National Information Technology Agency [put its draft Data Harmonisation Bill 2025 out for public consultation](<https://nita.gov.gh/publicconsultation-3-2-2/>) on 19 November 2025. In the last twelve months, in May 2026 the bill was [before Parliament and had not passed](<https://labarijournal.com/ghana-is-considering-passing-a-host-of-new-ict-related-laws-an-analyst-says-they-would-hamper-africa-digital-trade/>). In July 2026 a representative of the communications minister said [a Data Exchange Act was also proposed](<https://thechronicle.com.gh/government-rolls-out-10-year-ai-implementation-roadmap-to-drive-jobs-economic-growth/>). No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

No stage is set. The only text found is a 2019 arrêté between the health and territorial administration ministries on vaccination and birth certificates. It covers one sector, which a law for one sector cannot place. Nothing found names a law, decree or draft on public bodies sharing data in general. No change has been found in the last twelve months. An interoperability framework issued as a decree or regulation would count. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force, however old.

Guinea-Bissau's national regulation on the interoperability of digital systems and platforms was [approved by Decree 27/2025 and published in the Official Bulletin of 31 October 2025](<https://wardip.gw/governo-aprova-regulamento-nacional-de-interoperabilidade-para-acelerar-a-transformacao-digital-na-guine-bissau/>). In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed: the regional digital project [announced the approval again in August 2026](<https://pt.linkedin.com/posts/wardip-guin%C3%A9-bissau_governo-aprova-regulamento-nacional-de-interoperabilidade-activity-7491768929355194368-Vk5Q>). Reports say it lets public bodies share information securely. They do not say it obliges bodies to share, to connect to a platform, or to stop asking people for what another body holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

Liberia's [Executive Order No. 163](<https://www.liberianobserver.com/news/boakai-s-executive-order-163-signals-digital-government-shift/article_7a31a87b-4fe2-4578-9ff7-b0224f3bf36a.html>), signed by President Boakai on 22 April 2026, mandates interoperable digital systems across ministries, agencies and commissions. No earlier instrument on the subject has been found. In the last twelve months the order introduced a government interoperability framework, and says data sharing is governed by formal agreements on access, use and accountability. Draft legislation to make the arrangement permanent is due within twelve months of the order. No law is in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

Morocco's framework bill known as Digital X.0, which covers interoperability among other subjects, was [under review by the General Secretariat of the Government in November 2025](<https://www.wearetech.africa/en/fils-uk/news/tech/morocco-drafts-landmark-law-to-govern-ai-data-and-digital-identity>). In the last twelve months, on 30 June 2026 the minister said [a bill on dematerialising administrative services was being drawn up](<https://maroc.ma/fr/actualites/une-administration-publique-prete-pour-lavenir-requiert-une-gouvernance-moderne-et-adaptee-aux>), to base public services on data exchange between administrations. Neither bill had been passed by the end of September 2026. No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

In September 2025 Madagascar's ministry of digital development [held a workshop to validate a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability](<https://newsmada.com/2025/09/13/signature-electronique-et-interoperabilite-madagascar-renforce-le-cadre-juridique/>). The draft would set up a framework, a digital governance unit and a national interoperability committee. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no adoption by the government is recorded. The report does not say the decree would oblige public bodies to exchange data or connect to a common platform. No law, decree or regulation on sharing has been found in force. Establishing would need such a decree to be in force.

Mozambique's [Decree 67/2017 of 1 December 2017](<https://www.intic.gov.mz/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/BR_188_I_SERIE_2017.pdf>) approves the regulation of the e-government interoperability framework. It obliges public bodies to share the data they hold, and to use the single platform. In the last twelve months, the regulator [described a review in December 2025](<https://techafricanews.com/2025/12/05/mozambique-prioritizes-data-governance-as-cornerstone-of-digital-sovereignty/>). A revised regulation [went to its final consultation on 11 June 2026](<https://intic.gov.mz/decorre-a-fase-final-da-revisao-do-regulamento-do-quadro-de-interoperabilidade-de-sistemas-de-governo-digital-em-mocambique/>). It was still not adopted on 23 October 2026. No rule made under the decree since 2023 has been found. Mature would need such a rule, or bodies named as exchanging data because the decree requires it.

Mauritania's [Decree 2022-009](<https://mtnima.gov.mr/sites/default/files/2024-02/D%C3%A9cret%20n%C2%B02022-009%20Relatif%20aux%20%C3%A9changes%20%C3%A9lectroniques%20entre%20les%20usagers%20et%20les%20autorit%C3%A9s%20administratives%20et%20entre%20les%20autorit%C3%A9s%20administratives_%5BJ.O%20n%C2%B01505%5D.pdf>), published in Official Journal no. 1505, governs electronic exchanges between users and administrative authorities, and between the authorities themselves. The Council of Ministers heard it on 3 November 2021. No change has been found in the last twelve months. It governs how exchanges are made. It is not recorded as obliging an authority to share data, to connect to a platform, or to stop asking users for what another authority holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

No stage is set. The only law found is a 2022 amendment to the Civil Status Act. It lets the Bank of Mauritius share population data for customer checks, which is one purpose. A law for one sector places nothing. Nothing found names a law, decree or draft on public bodies sharing data in general. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force, however old.

In June 2026 Malawi's Ministry of Information and Communications Technology [proposed a Government Data Sharing Regulation](<https://itweb.africa/article/malawi-devises-operational-rules-for-national-data-exchange-platform/xnklOvz1R2bq4Ymz>) to govern the national data exchange platform, Boma Lathu. In the last twelve months this is the only text found, and the regulation had not been made by the end of September 2026. The minister said government institutions still share citizens' data by email, on USB drives and on paper. No instrument in force requires public bodies to exchange data. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

Niger's [Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions](<https://mcnti.gouv.ne/ova_doc/loi-2019-03-du-30-avril-2019-portant-sur-les-transactions-electroniques-au-niger/>) lets administrations exchange information electronically in Article 29. Article 35 institutes a General Interoperability Framework, to be set by decree, and its norms and standards are those the administration must use. Article 33 exempts an applicant from supplying a document the administration can obtain directly. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No regulation or order made under the law has been found, and no public body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to. Mature would need such a rule, or bodies named as exchanging data under it.

On 26 March 2026 Senegal's digital ministry said the first phase of its interoperability work had [delivered a national interoperability framework, a draft decree and a platform](<https://fr.linkedin.com/posts/mctnsn_newdealtechnologique-interop%C3%A9rabilit%C3%A9-activity-7443068023738900480-ejtp>). In the last twelve months, on 4 May 2026 it announced that [the draft decree governing the interoperability platform would be presented the next day](<https://fr.linkedin.com/posts/mctnsn_dpi-newdealtechnologique-activity-7457180609757528065-UqRT>). No adoption is recorded. The posts do not say the decree would oblige public bodies to connect to the platform or to exchange data through it. No law, decree or regulation on sharing is in force. Establishing would need such a decree to be in force.

On 29 September 2024 GovStack [stated that Somalia has no enabling legislation for data sharing and data analysis](<https://govstack.global/showcase/digital-leaders-spotlight-rwanda/>). No change has been found in the last twelve months. No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is recorded in force, and no draft of one is recorded. Nothing found shows whether public bodies are required to share data. Preparing would need a bill, draft decree or draft regulation on public bodies sharing data to be published, before parliament or cabinet, or passed and not yet in force.

A legal survey of 2024 [cites Law 1/2024](<https://www.ibanet.org/document?id=Digital-Regulations-in-the-Metaverse-Era-Sao-Tome-Principe>) as the national framework for interoperability in Sao Tome and Principe. It says the framework addresses data sharing and data governance in public institutions. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed: in October 2026 the justice minister [cited Law 1/2024 among the country's legislative initiatives](<https://rafa.tl/pt/sao-tome-e-principe-defende-mecanismos-mais-rapidos-para-obter-provas-digitais-entre-paises-da-cplp/>). The survey does not say the law obliges public bodies to share data or to connect to a platform. No regulation or order made under the law has been found. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

Tunisia's [Government Decree 2020-777 of 5 October 2020](<https://legislation-securite.tn/latest-laws/decret-gouvernemental-n-2020-777-du-5-octobre-2020-fixant-les-conditions-les-modalites-et-les-procedures-dapplication-du-decret-loi-du-chef-du-gouvernement-n-2020-31-du-10-juin/>) sets the conditions for applying Decree-Law 2020-31 of 10 June 2020. It says public structures must use electronic exchange among themselves and with their users. In the last twelve months the decree-law was cited and not changed: the Presidency of the Government [gave it as in force in October 2026](<https://www.alchourouk.com/index.php/article/%D8%B1%D8%A6%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%83%D9%88%D9%85%D8%A9-%D9%8A%D8%AA%D9%85-%D8%AD%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D9%85%D9%84-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%83%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A%D8%B2-%D9%85%D9%86%D8%B5%D8%A9-%D9%84%D8%AA%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AF%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B9%D8%B7%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%83%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D9%85%D9%88%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A9>). No rule made under it since 2023 has been found. Mature would need such a rule, or bodies named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

Tanzania's [e-Government Act, No. 10 of 2019](<https://oagmis.oag.go.tz/portal/acts/revised/559/download>) started on 19 September 2019 and applies to all public institutions. Section 48 provides for data sharing and exchange between public institutions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says the Act obliges other public institutions to share data or to connect to the government's exchange system. Nothing found says it stops them asking people for what another institution already holds. No regulation or order on data sharing made under the Act since 2023 has been found. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

Uganda's [National Information Technology Authority-Uganda (E-Government) Regulations, 2015](<https://pmlawhub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/NITA-U-E-Government-Regulations-2015-SI-No.-27-of-2015.pdf>) were made by the ICT Minister on 4 May 2015 and gazetted on 10 June 2015. They bind all public bodies and make use of the shared government backbone mandatory. On information sharing, regulation 13 says bodies may share. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says public bodies must share data, connect to an exchange platform, or stop asking a person for what another body holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

South Africa's [Public Service Regulations, 2016](<https://www.dpsa.gov.za/dpsa2g/documents/acts&regulations/regulations2016/PUBLIC%20service%20regulations%2016%20April%202019.pdf>) took effect on 1 August 2016. The Minister for the Public Service and Administration made them under the Public Service Act. Chapter 6 carries a regulation 97 headed *Minimum interoperability standards*. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the law in force requires public bodies to share data or to connect to the government's exchange platform. None says it bars them from asking a person for what another public body already holds. Operating would need a law, decree or regulation that requires public bodies to share.

Zambia's [Electronic Government Act, No. 41 of 2021](<https://www.parliament.gov.zm/sites/default/files/documents/acts/Act%20No.%2041%20OF%202021%2C%20THE%20ELECTRONIC%20GOVERNMENT%20ACT%2C%202021_0.pdf>) was assented to on 19 May 2021. It lets public bodies share data and does not require it. In the last twelve months, in January 2026 [an amendment bill was presented to stakeholders](<https://itweb.africa/article/zambia-begins-amending-electronic-government-act/>). It is described as giving legal standing to electronic submissions and digital authentication. No regulation made under the Act since 2023 has been found. No public body is named as exchanging data because the Act requires it. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.
